title: Perimeter I: Cloud NGFW, Cloud Armor, IAP, Load Balancer TLS and Certificate Authority Service

concepts.heading: Cloud NGFW: Policies, Rules and Tiers
concepts.body: Cloud NGFW is a distributed, stateful firewall that applies rules to VM network interfaces and to supported load balancers. Rules live in policies: hierarchical policies attach to the organization or a folder, and global or regional network policies attach to a VPC network. A rule's action decides what happens next. Allow and deny stop evaluation, so an organization-level deny cannot be overridden below, while goto_next hands the decision to the next step, which lets a project team decide. A company that must block Telnet everywhere but leave SSH to each project writes a deny for tcp:23 and a goto_next for tcp:22 at the top. Rules can target secure tags or service accounts instead of IP ranges, which gives micro-segmentation that follows the workload. Features come in three tiers. Essentials matches IP ranges, ports and protocols. Standard adds FQDN objects and threat intelligence. Enterprise adds Layer 7 security: intrusion prevention, URL filtering and TLS inspection. For internal Application Load Balancers and internal proxy Network Load Balancers, network firewall policies provide Layer 3 and Layer 4 filtering.

concepts.heading: Layer 7 Inspection and TLS Inspection
concepts.body: Intrusion prevention and URL filtering run on firewall endpoints, Google-managed zonal resources that inspect intercepted traffic. A firewall policy rule with the apply_security_profile_group action sends matching packets to the endpoint, and the threat-prevention security profile in the group defines which signatures are scanned and what happens on a match. An endpoint inspects traffic in its own zone, so workloads in two zones need an endpoint in each. URL filtering matches the host header for plain HTTP, only the plaintext SNI for HTTPS without TLS inspection, and the host header together with the SNI once TLS inspection decrypts the traffic. TLS inspection decrypts, inspects and re-encrypts toward the destination, using short-lived certificates issued through Certificate Authority Service. It needs a CA pool and a TLS inspection policy, and both are regional, so a deployment in two regions needs two of each. Clients must trust the root of that CA or they see certificate errors. The trade-off is plain: decryption shows the rules more, and in return you must distribute a root certificate to every client.

concepts.heading: Cloud Armor and Identity-Aware Proxy at the Front Door
concepts.body: Cloud Armor security policies filter requests at the edge of Google's network for external Application Load Balancers and other supported endpoints. A backend security policy covers requests that reach the backend service. An edge security policy sits upstream of the Cloud CDN cache and supports fewer parameters, so it can deny an abusive range even for objects that would be served from cache. Start new preconfigured WAF rules, which are compiled from OWASP signatures, in preview mode: matches are logged but not enforced, so false positives can be tuned first. Rate-based ban rules count requests per key such as XFF_IP and ban abusers for a set period. Adaptive Protection detects Layer 7 anomalies, but full alerts with a signature and suggested rule need Cloud Armor Enterprise. Identity-Aware Proxy adds identity: it authenticates the caller and checks IAM for the IAP-secured Web App User role, best granted to a group so joiners and leavers need no IAM edits. If backends are reachable directly, callers bypass IAP, so firewall rules should admit only the load balancer and health check ranges. Scripts send an OIDC ID token for a service account.

concepts.heading: TLS Policy, Certificates and Private CAs
concepts.body: An SSL policy sets the minimum TLS version and cipher profile for connections between clients and the load balancer, not toward the backends. Without a policy the load balancer behaves as COMPATIBLE with a minimum of TLS 1.0, so a requirement of TLS 1.2 needs one. The RESTRICTED profile narrows the cipher set. A SaaS company that terminates HTTPS for thousands of customer domains and renews certificates often uses Certificate Manager: Google-managed or self-managed certificates, selected by host name through a certificate map on the target proxy. For private PKI, Certificate Authority Service creates root and subordinate CAs. The tier belongs to the CA pool. DevOps suits high-volume, short-lived certificates that need no revocation. Enterprise supports revocation and certificate storage and is recommended for pools that issue to other CAs, so mTLS between microservices with revocable certificates belongs there. A company that keeps its root CA offline on premises can create subordinate CAs in CA Service that chain to that root, so trust stays anchored offline while the cloud CAs issue day to day.

examPoints: A question that blocks a range even for objects served from Cloud CDN points to a Cloud Armor edge security policy, and one that wants to see false positives before blocking points to a new rule in preview mode.

A question where a deny must hold at the top while a lower level still decides another port points to a hierarchical firewall policy with deny and goto_next, and one asking for threat signatures or URL filtering points to the Cloud NGFW Enterprise tier with firewall endpoints per zone.

A question about revocable certificates, subordinate CAs or an offline root points to Certificate Authority Service Enterprise pools, and one about thousands of customer domains points to Certificate Manager with a certificate map.

quiz.q: A video site serves segments through a global external Application Load Balancer with Cloud CDN. A Cloud Armor backend policy with WAF rules exists, yet one abusive address range keeps pulling cached segments. What blocks it?
choices: A higher priority deny rule for that range in the existing backend security policy, which sees every cached request
Adaptive Protection on the existing backend policy, which blocks the range automatically once it detects the traffic
A Cloud Armor edge security policy with a deny rule for that range, attached to the backend service
An Identity-Aware Proxy access list on the backend service, which stops callers outside the approved identity group
quiz.explain: The edge policy is enforced upstream of the Cloud CDN cache, so it can deny the range even for objects that would be served from cache. The backend policy is enforced only for requests that reach the backend, so cache hits never meet its rules. Adaptive Protection alerts and suggests a rule but blocks nothing by itself, and IAP checks identity, not an address range.

quiz.q: A security team must stop Telnet to every VM at the organization level, while each project team stays free to decide about SSH with its own rules. Which hierarchical firewall policy rules do this?
choices: A deny rule for tcp:23 and a goto_next rule for tcp:22, so project-level rules decide on SSH
An allow rule for tcp:22 and a deny rule for tcp:23, so every project inherits one fixed answer
A goto_next rule for tcp:23 and a deny rule for tcp:22, so project teams choose about Telnet
A deny rule for tcp:23 and a deny rule for tcp:22, so no project below can open either port
quiz.explain: A deny at the top cannot be overridden below, and goto_next passes the decision to the next step in the order, where project rules sit, so they decide on SSH. An allow at the top ends evaluation and takes the decision away from the projects. Swapping the actions delegates the wrong port. Denying both ports removes the SSH decision from the project teams.

recap: At the perimeter, pick the layer for the threat: Cloud NGFW for VPC traffic (Enterprise for Layer 7), Cloud Armor and IAP at the load balancer front door, an SSL policy and Certificate Manager for TLS, and Certificate Authority Service for private PKI.

title: Perimeter II: Public versus Private IP, Secure Web Proxy, Cloud DNS Security and API Restrictions

concepts.heading: Public versus Private IP Addresses
concepts.body: A Compute Engine VM is reachable from the internet only when it has an external address and a firewall rule admits the traffic. A security engineer removes the two conditions with separate controls, so one mistake does not expose a workload. Organization policy removes the address: the Restrict External IPs For VM instances constraint, constraints/compute.managed.vmExternalIpAccess, denies creating or updating VMs with IPv4 external addresses. Specific instances can be exempted by tagging them and scoping the enforcement with conditions on the tag; the older list constraint, constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess, instead lists the allowed instances. Firewall policy removes the second condition, and the implied deny ingress rule already blocks unsolicited inbound traffic. The managed constraint covers IPv4 only. A dual-stack subnet with an external IPv6 access type still gives a VM a publicly routable IPv6 address, so private workloads belong in subnets with internal IPv6 access, backed by ingress deny rules. Administrators then reach private VMs through Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding, which needs the IAP-secured Tunnel User role, and outbound access comes from Private Google Access, Cloud NAT or Secure Web Proxy instead of a public address on every machine.

concepts.heading: Secure Web Proxy for Outbound Web Traffic
concepts.body: Secure Web Proxy is a managed outbound proxy for HTTP and HTTPS. In explicit proxy mode clients are configured to use it (next hop mode routes traffic to it instead), and it denies all outbound traffic until a rule allows it, so a missing rule fails safely. Policies are separate from the proxy, so one URL list or set of gateway security rules can be reused across proxies, and rules can match sources such as IP addresses, service accounts or secure tags. Without decryption an HTTPS request exposes only the host name. A bank that must allow www.example.com/documentation but block www.example.com/uploads therefore needs TLS inspection: the proxy presents certificates issued from a private CA pool in Certificate Authority Service, and clients must trust that root, which suits managed devices. Clients that pin certificates, such as operating system updaters, reject the proxy's certificate, so the session matcher excludes their destinations from decryption instead of switching inspection off for everyone. With Shared VPC the proxy is deployed in the host project, and it supports IPv4 only. Allowed traffic typically leaves through Cloud NAT, and activity is logged for audit.

concepts.heading: Cloud DNS Security
concepts.body: Cloud DNS has three security tools. DNSSEC signs a public zone so resolvers can detect forged or poisoned answers. It authenticates answers and does not encrypt queries, and it works only as a chain: Cloud DNS signs the zone, the registrar must publish a matching DS record in the parent zone, and the client's resolver must validate. A zone that shows DNSSEC as on but has no DS record at the registrar protects nobody. Response policies override answers inside a VPC network. A wildcard rule for *.malware-campaign.test can return a sinkhole address, and a passthru rule exempts one required subdomain so it resolves normally. Only one response policy can be attached to a network, but it can hold many rules. Query logging is switched on through a DNS policy on the network and records the names resolved by VMs, GKE containers and on-premises clients using inbound forwarding, written to Cloud Logging under the project that owns the network. That is where DNS tunnelling shows up as random-looking names, because flow logs record IP connections and audit logs record API calls. Routing policies steer traffic and are not a security control.

concepts.heading: Restricting and Monitoring API Use
concepts.body: The Restrict Resource Service Usage constraint, constraints/gcp.restrictServiceUsage, allows or denies Google Cloud services for an organization, folder or project, either as a denylist or as an allowlist but not both. It does not apply to essential dependencies such as IAM, Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring, and services that depend directly on a restricted service are restricted too: denying Compute Engine also stops GKE. The effect is immediate, so Google suggests enforcing it conditionally with tags and widening scope gradually. The second control is the API key. A standard key identifies a project for quota and billing, not a principal, so IAM cannot limit who uses it, and a key embedded in a published Android app should be assumed extractable. Use two restrictions together. An API restriction limits the key to listed APIs, for example only the Places API. An application restriction limits where the key is accepted: websites by HTTP referrer, IP addresses, Android apps by package name and signing certificate fingerprint, or iOS apps by bundle identifier. A key with no application restriction works from anywhere. Review usage metrics and quota consumption per key to notice abuse.

examPoints: A question where private VMs still become reachable after IPv4 external addresses were denied points to the constraint covering IPv4 only, so the fix is internal IPv6 access plus ingress deny rules.

A question that allows one URL path and blocks another over HTTPS points to Secure Web Proxy with TLS inspection, and one about update clients that reject the proxy certificate points to session matcher exclusions.

A question about DNS lookups of random-looking names points to query logging through a DNS policy, one about a sinkhole with one exempted subdomain points to a response policy with passthru, and one about an embedded mobile key points to API and application restrictions.

quiz.q: A bank's managed VMs must download packages from www.example.com/documentation, but traffic to www.example.com/uploads must be blocked, and both are HTTPS requests leaving the VPC. Which design works?
choices: Secure Web Proxy without decryption, with a host rule for www.example.com that the proxy applies to each request path
A Cloud NGFW egress rule from the Standard tier that matches the FQDN object for www.example.com and then filters the path
A Cloud DNS response policy that returns a sinkhole address only for requests made to the uploads path on that host
Secure Web Proxy with TLS inspection from a CA Service pool, the root trusted on the VMs, and URL rules
quiz.explain: Without decryption an HTTPS request exposes only the host name, so a rule on the path is possible only after the proxy terminates TLS and inspects the request. That needs a certificate issued from a private CA that the managed VMs trust. A host rule cannot tell the two paths apart, an FQDN object matches names and not paths, and DNS answers are keyed by name, never by URL path.

quiz.q: Security operations suspects that a compromised GKE workload leaks data through DNS lookups of random-looking names resolved inside the VPC network. Flow logs only show connections to the resolver. What gives visibility into the names?
choices: VPC Flow Logs on the cluster subnet with a higher sampling rate, since the logs also record the names being resolved
Query logging enabled by a Cloud DNS policy on the VPC network, with entries read in Cloud Logging
Cloud Audit Logs Data Access entries for Cloud DNS, because they record each lookup made by a workload in the network
A Cloud DNS routing policy with geolocation records on the zone, which tags each lookup with the name that was queried
quiz.explain: Cloud DNS query logging, switched on by a DNS policy on the network, records the queries the network's resolver handles, including those from GKE containers, and writes them to Cloud Logging where sinks and alerts can use them. Flow logs record IP connections, not names, even when sampled more. Audit logs record API calls, not lookups. Routing policies steer answers and add no query visibility.

recap: Keep workloads private with two independent controls (no external address, no admitting firewall rule), send outbound web traffic through Secure Web Proxy, protect and log DNS, and limit Google API use with the service usage constraint and restricted API keys.

title: VPC Service Controls: Perimeters, Access Levels, Ingress and Egress Rules, Dry Run

concepts.heading: What a Perimeter Protects
concepts.body: A VPC Service Controls perimeter surrounds projects, and optionally VPC networks, so that the Google-managed services you list as restricted, such as Cloud Storage and BigQuery, cannot exchange data with anything outside it. It is a layer independent of IAM: IAM says who may call, while the perimeter says from where and toward which projects. That is why it helps when credentials are stolen, when a misconfigured IAM policy exposes a dataset, or when an insider or compromised code tries to copy data out. Service operations such as gcloud storage cp to a public bucket or bq mk to an external BigQuery table are blocked at the boundary. A firewall cannot do this, because every bucket, including an attacker's, sits behind the same storage.googleapis.com endpoint. In enforced mode violations are denied. Access from the internet is denied by default, and the Google Cloud console is blocked until an access level admits it. The service complements IAM and does not replace it.

concepts.heading: Access Levels and Ingress Rules
concepts.body: Two mechanisms admit requests from outside. An access level, created in Access Context Manager, classifies a request by attributes such as source IP range, region, identity and device policy. Device data comes from Endpoint Verification, with criteria such as screen lock, storage encryption and operating system version, and conditions in one level are combined, so a request must satisfy all of them. Analysts on changing home addresses suit a device-policy level better than IP ranges. An ingress rule is more granular. Its from block names identities and sources (an access level, a project or a VPC network), and its to block names services, methods or permissions and target projects. A partner's service account that must read one BigQuery dataset gets a rule that names that identity, the read methods and the owning project, instead of a level that admits a whole address range. A developer VM in an unprotected project that is blocked from a protected bucket needs an ingress rule with the caller's project as the source, because a private IP address alone is ambiguous. Ingress and egress rules replace many cases that once needed perimeter bridges.

concepts.heading: Egress, Shared VPC and Accessible Services
concepts.body: Direction describes the request, not the data flow. A VM inside the perimeter that writes a nightly export to an auditor's bucket is egress, so an egress rule must name that service account, the target project and the object-creation methods, and every other copy to an outside bucket stays blocked. Access levels and ingress rules never authorize a call that leaves the perimeter. A request touching resources on both sides can need both rule types. An analyst outside the perimeter who runs a BigQuery job in an outside project against a dataset inside needs an ingress rule for the analyst and an egress rule for the outside job project, and the audit log shows both violations when one is missing. Shared VPC adds a trap: VMs in service projects use the host project's network, so put the host project in the same perimeter, or requests look as if they come from a network outside it. VPC accessible services limits what endpoints inside the perimeter may call, for example only Cloud Storage and BigQuery. A call to anything else is denied and logged as SERVICE_NOT_ALLOWED_FROM_VPC.

concepts.heading: Dry Run and Access Policies
concepts.body: A new restriction can break workloads, so test it in dry run. A perimeter holds an enforced configuration and a dry run configuration. Dry run violations are logged with metadata.dryRun set to true and are not denied. The dry run configuration starts as a copy of the enforced one, and only requests that the enforced configuration allows but the dry run configuration would deny appear as dry run violations. Access levels have no dry run mode, so to test a change you create a new access level and attach it only to the dry run configuration. A project can be in one enforced and one dry run configuration, not necessarily of the same perimeter. To trial moving a project from perimeter PA to PB, remove it from PA's dry run configuration and add it to PB's. Read denials in the audit log by violationReason: NETWORK_NOT_IN_SAME_SERVICE_PERIMETER points to an ingress or egress rule for a network, and NO_MATCHING_ACCESS_LEVEL to an internet caller that matched nothing. An organization has one organization-level access policy, and scoped policies let a business unit manage its own folder.

examPoints: A question about copying data to a bucket in an attacker's project, despite correct IAM and firewall rules, points to a VPC Service Controls perimeter, because only it checks which project owns the resource being called.

A question that shares one dataset with a partner points to an identity-based ingress rule with narrow methods and target project, and one about a VM writing to an auditor's bucket points to a narrow egress rule.

A question about testing a new restricted service or access level before enforcing points to the dry run configuration with a new access level, and one about Shared VPC failures points to the host project joining the perimeter.

quiz.q: A perimeter is enforced around analytics projects. The team wants to add the Cloud KMS API as a restricted service and admit requests from a new office network, and must see what would break before any user is affected. What should they do?
choices: Edit the existing access level in place and turn on its dry run mode, then read the violations it logs for the perimeter
Change the enforced configuration at once, because the audit log reports requests that were denied and can be reverted
Create a second perimeter for the same projects in enforced mode, and keep both until the denied requests are compared
Change the dry run configuration, add a new access level for the office to it, and review the logged dry run violations
quiz.explain: A dry run configuration can be changed freely without affecting enforcement, and its violations are logged with the dry run flag. Access levels have no dry run mode of their own, so the change is made as a new access level attached to the dry run configuration. Editing the enforced configuration affects users immediately. A project can be in only one enforced configuration, so a second enforced perimeter is not possible.

quiz.q: A research partner's service account in the partner's own organization must read one BigQuery dataset in a project inside an enforced perimeter. What is the most precise, least-privilege way to allow it?
choices: An access level admitting the partner's published IP ranges, attached to the perimeter for every restricted service
An ingress rule naming that service account, the BigQuery read methods and the owning project as the target
A perimeter bridge joining the partner's project to the perimeter, so projects on both sides can reach each other
An egress rule that lets the dataset's project call the partner's project for the BigQuery read operations
quiz.explain: An ingress rule can be narrowed by identity, method and target project, so only that account gets only read access to one project regardless of its source address. An access level admits by attributes such as IP range and is far broader. Perimeter bridges are bidirectional and cannot include projects from different organizations. Egress describes requests leaving the perimeter, which is the wrong direction for this call.

recap: A VPC Service Controls perimeter is the control for data exfiltration through Google APIs: admit outsiders with narrow ingress rules, allow exits with narrow egress rules, keep Shared VPC host and service projects together, and test every change in dry run.

title: Segmentation: VPC Security Properties, Peering, Shared VPC, Firewall Rules and N-tier Isolation

concepts.heading: VPC Building Blocks and Defaults
concepts.body: A VPC network is a global resource and its subnets are regional. Auto mode networks create one subnet in every region from predefined ranges inside 10.128.0.0/9, while custom mode networks contain only the subnets you define, so you can plan ranges that do not overlap with peered or on-premises networks. Two auto mode networks cannot even be peered, because their ranges collide. Every network has two implied rules at the lowest priority: allow all egress and deny all ingress. The default network that a new project receives also comes with pre-populated rules that allow certain ingress traffic. Enforcing constraints/compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation on a folder skips creating that default network and its supporting resources, so teams build custom mode networks with explicit rules instead. A sound checklist for a new project is therefore no default network, custom mode subnets, explicit allow rules between tiers, and organization policy against external IPs and IP forwarding. The implied deny ingress is the safety net, not the design: write the rules you intend, so the allowed paths are visible and auditable.

concepts.heading: N-tier Isolation
concepts.body: Segmentation between web, application and database tiers comes from allowing only adjacent tiers to talk: web to app on the app port, app to database on the database port, and everything else falls to the implied deny. Write sources and targets as service accounts or secure tags rather than IP ranges, so rules follow the workload when it scales or moves. Secure tags in network firewall policies are the micro-segmentation tool, and hierarchical firewall policies set guardrails above the projects. Rule actions decide who has the last word: allow and deny stop evaluation, and goto_next delegates downward. A relay path is another way around tiers. When IP forwarding is enabled, a VM can forward packets for other addresses, so the Restrict VM IP forwarding constraint, constraints/compute.managed.vmCanIpForward, denies it for a folder, and approved network appliances get an override on their own project. Firewall rules match packet addresses and ports and cannot know that a VM is acting as a relay. Finally, firewalls cannot separate a company bucket from an attacker's bucket, because both are the same API endpoint. That boundary belongs to VPC Service Controls.

concepts.heading: VPC Network Peering
concepts.body: VPC Network Peering joins two networks over internal addresses but keeps them administratively separate. Only routes are exchanged, according to each side's settings, and firewall rules and policies are not. Peering is not transitive: if net-a peers with net-b and with net-c, there is no path between net-b and net-c. Each network enforces its own implied deny ingress, so a database network that wants only the application subnet 10.20.0.0/24 on tcp:5432 writes one ingress allow rule with that source range. Egress to the peer needs no rule unless a deny exists. Network tags and service accounts in VPC firewall rules resolve only to instances in the rule's own network, so a peer's tag never matches. Use the peer's IP range instead, or a secure tag as the source in a network firewall policy, which can identify sources in the tag's network and in networks peered with it. By default a network admin can peer with any other network, so the Restrict VPC peering usage constraint, constraints/compute.restrictVpcPeering, lists the networks that may be peered, for example everything under the organization. It acts before the peering exists, unlike an audit alert.

concepts.heading: Shared VPC and Separation of Duties
concepts.body: Shared VPC fits one organization that wants central control of the network and delegated compute administration. A host project owns the Shared VPC network, service projects attach to it and each service project has a single host. A project cannot be both host and service, and participating projects must belong to the same organization. Roles split the duties. The Shared VPC Admin enables host projects and attaches service projects. Network Admin on the host project controls network resources except firewall rules and SSL certificates. Security Admin on the host project manages firewall rules and SSL certificates. Service project admins hold Compute Network User on specific subnets and can create instances without changing the network. Granting that role per subnet instead of on the whole host project gives each team its own slice. Two constraints add guardrails: constraints/compute.restrictSharedVpcHostProjects limits which hosts a project, folder or organization can attach to, and constraints/compute.restrictSharedVpcSubnetworks limits which shared subnets service projects may use for new VMs and load balancers. Choose Shared VPC for central administration and peering where networks stay separately administered.

examPoints: A question about a peer network's tag that never matches points to firewall rules resolving tags and service accounts only inside their own network, so the rule needs the peer's IP range or a secure tag as source.

A question about stopping teams from peering with outside networks before the connection exists points to the Restrict VPC peering usage constraint, and one about new projects with permissive default rules points to skipping default network creation.

A question about separating who manages routes from who manages firewall rules in Shared VPC points to Network Admin and Security Admin on the host project, with Compute Network User granted per subnet.

quiz.q: Two peered networks, net-app and net-db, host the application and database tiers. An administrator of net-db wrote an ingress allow rule for tcp:5432 whose source is the network tag app-tier, yet application VMs in net-app cannot connect. What fixes this with the least exposure?
choices: Use the application subnet's range as source, since network tags resolve only inside the rule's own network
Create the same app-tier tag on the database VMs, because peered networks share tags through the peering configuration
Add an egress allow rule in net-app for tcp:5432, because the implied egress rule is removed by peering for those VMs
Allow tcp:5432 from 0.0.0.0/0 in net-db, because peering already restricts traffic to the two peered networks
quiz.explain: Network tags in a VPC firewall rule resolve only to instances in the rule's own network, so the peer's tag matches nothing. A rule with the application subnet's range as source admits exactly that tier. Peering does not share tags or merge firewall rules, and egress is allowed by the implied rule unless an egress deny exists. Opening the port to every address gives up the segmentation that the design was meant to deliver.

quiz.q: A company runs Shared VPC and wants network administrators to control subnets and routes, but only the security team to change firewall rules and SSL certificates. Which grant on the host project does this?
choices: Shared VPC Admin for both teams, because that role is the only one that manages firewall rules in a host project
Compute Network User for both teams on every shared subnet, with firewall rules left at the project defaults
Network Admin for the network team and Security Admin for the security team, both granted on the host project
Network Admin for both teams on the host project, because it already covers firewall rules and SSL certificates
quiz.explain: Network Admin has full control of network resources except firewall rules and SSL certificates, and Security Admin is the role that manages those, so splitting the two roles separates the duties. Shared VPC Admin enables host projects and attaches service projects, and it is not meant for daily firewall work. Compute Network User only lets a team use subnets. Network Admin deliberately excludes firewall rules.

recap: Segment with custom mode networks, tier-to-tier allow rules based on service accounts or secure tags, and organization policy guardrails, then choose peering for separately administered networks and Shared VPC for central control with split Network and Security Admin duties.

title: Private Connectivity: Private Google Access, Private Service Connect, HA VPN, Interconnect and Cloud NAT

concepts.heading: Private Google Access, Private and Restricted Ranges
concepts.body: A VM with only an internal address reaches Google APIs when Private Google Access is enabled on its subnet (a per-subnet setting that does not affect VMs with external addresses). On-premises hosts take another path: they send API traffic to a virtual IP range over Cloud VPN or VLAN attachments, and the subnet setting is not needed. Two domains exist. private.googleapis.com, 199.36.153.8/30, reaches most Google APIs, including ones that VPC Service Controls does not support. restricted.googleapis.com, 199.36.153.4/30, reaches only APIs that VPC Service Controls supports, so a regulated client cannot fall back to an unprotected API. DNS chooses the range, and each client population should resolve to exactly one of them, because mixed answers cause intermittent failures. Google publishes no routes for these ranges, so Cloud Router advertises the range to on premises as a custom advertised route, and the VPC network needs a custom static route to it with the default internet gateway as next hop. It restores access to just that range if the default route was deleted. Responses return through attachments in the region of the request, so keep attachments in each such region.

concepts.heading: Private Service Connect
concepts.body: Private Service Connect gives private access to services through addresses you control. An endpoint for Google APIs is a forwarding rule with an internal IP address in your VPC network that maps to an API bundle: all-apis, or vpc-sc for the services VPC Service Controls supports. Unlike Private Google Access you choose the address and can create one per team, and on-premises hosts reach it over Cloud VPN or VLAN attachments. DNS decides whether it is used. The endpoint creates names such as storage-logs1.p.googleapis.com in a private zone, and a client whose lookup misses that zone falls through to public DNS and connects publicly. Backends put your own load balancer in front of a service attachment or Google API, which gives custom domains and certificates, Cloud Armor and control of regional failover. For Google-managed services such as Cloud SQL, an endpoint avoids the allocated range and VPC Network Peering of private services access, and peering is not transitive. A producer's service attachment can accept connections only from an accept list. A connection stays Pending, with no traffic flowing, when its project is not on the accept list or when the connections exceed the service attachment's connection limit.

concepts.heading: Encrypting Hybrid Links: HA VPN and MACsec
concepts.body: Cloud VPN protects traffic with IPsec, and its tunnels cross the public internet. HA VPN uses dynamic routing with BGP. Cloud Interconnect gives a private path, but encryption is something you add, and the two options work at different layers. MACsec for Cloud Interconnect, IEEE 802.1AE, encrypts at layer 2 between your on-premises router and Google's edge routers, using keys you configure on your router. It does not provide encryption in transit within Google, so Google recommends layering it with IPsec and TLS. On Partner Interconnect the provider's network is in the path, so MACsec has to be arranged with the service provider. When a policy asks for network-layer encryption end to end between your networks and the VPC, use HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect: IPsec tunnels over the VLAN attachments, which keep the private Interconnect path and give layer 3 encryption. A retailer with Dedicated Interconnect and that policy chooses HA VPN over Interconnect, and an enterprise that only needs the link between routers protected can choose MACsec. The two can be combined for defense in depth.

concepts.heading: Cloud NAT for Controlled Egress
concepts.body: Cloud NAT gives resources without external IP addresses outbound access to internet destinations. It is a distributed, software-defined service configured on a Cloud Router, with no proxy VMs or appliances in the path. A gateway translates only the subnets or subnet ranges you select, so scope it to the subnets that need it. In a project with build VMs and sensitive data-processing VMs, a gateway serving only the build subnet leaves the sensitive VMs with no external address and no translation, and the external IP constraint stops anyone adding one by mistake. Cloud NAT translates established inbound response packets only and never allows unsolicited inbound connections. Many VMs share a few external addresses, so a partner reporting scanning from one cannot name the VM. Cloud NAT logging in Cloud Logging, set to record translations, ties the external address and port to the internal VM. Logging only errors would miss connections that succeeded.  The Restrict Cloud NAT usage constraint, constraints/compute.restrictCloudNATUsage, limits which subnetworks may use Cloud NAT.

examPoints: A question where on-premises clients must reach only Google APIs that VPC Service Controls protects points to restricted.googleapis.com resolved by on-premises DNS and advertised through Cloud Router, and one with intermittent failures points to DNS mixing the two ranges.

A question about an internal address from the consumer's own subnet for a Google API or a managed service points to a Private Service Connect endpoint, and one where the endpoint exists but traffic goes public points to a missing private DNS answer.

A question about network-layer encryption over Dedicated Interconnect points to HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect, one about protecting only the hop between routers points to MACsec, and one about tracing a shared NAT address points to Cloud NAT translation logging.

quiz.q: An insurer's on-premises servers call Cloud Storage and BigQuery over HA VPN tunnels. VPC Service Controls protects the data projects, and the servers must be unable to reach any Google API that VPC Service Controls cannot protect. Which design meets this?
choices: Resolve Google API names to private.googleapis.com on premises and advertise that range from the Cloud Router
Resolve Google API names to restricted.googleapis.com on premises and advertise that range from the Cloud Router
Enable Private Google Access on the subnets that end the tunnels, since it also covers requests from on premises
Give each server a public route to Google APIs, then deny external requests with VPC Service Controls ingress rules
quiz.explain: The restricted range serves only the APIs that VPC Service Controls supports, so unprotected APIs become unreachable, and advertising it from Cloud Router keeps the traffic on the tunnels. The private range reaches most APIs, including unprotected ones. For on-premises hosts the subnet setting is not what makes access work. A public route leaves the internet path open.

quiz.q: A retailer uses Dedicated Interconnect. A new policy requires all traffic between its on-premises networks and the VPC networks to be encrypted at the network layer, end to end. What should the network team deploy?
choices: MACsec on the Dedicated Interconnect ports, which encrypts traffic from the on-premises router into the VPC
A Private Service Connect endpoint for Google APIs, which wraps each connection to the VPC in a private tunnel
Cloud NAT on the VPC subnets, which translates addresses so that on-premises traffic appears from a new range
HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect, with IPsec tunnels built across the VLAN attachments of the existing links
quiz.explain: IPsec tunnels over the VLAN attachments give layer 3 encryption between the networks while keeping the private path. MACsec works at layer 2 between the on-premises router and Google's edge routers and does not provide encryption in transit within Google. A Private Service Connect endpoint is an address for reaching a service and does not encrypt a link. Cloud NAT only translates addresses.

recap: Reach Google APIs and managed services privately with Private Google Access ranges (restricted for VPC Service Controls) or Private Service Connect endpoints, encrypt hybrid links with HA VPN over Interconnect or MACsec, and scope Cloud NAT to the subnets that need egress.
